title: First-Sighting Letter Cipher
statement:
A substitution cipher is defined by a string key made of lowercase letters and spaces. It contains every letter of the alphabet at least once.

Read key from left to right and look only at the first time each letter appears. The first new letter stands for a, the second new letter for b, and so on up to z. Spaces and repeated letters in the key are skipped.

Decode message with this table: replace each letter with the letter it stands for. Spaces stay spaces. Return the decoded string.

examples.in:
key = "pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs"
message = "omttv rvztk"
examples.why: The first sightings are p, a, c, k, m, y, b, o, … so o is the 8th new letter and stands for h, m is the 5th and stands for e, and so on.
A reversed alphabet: z stands for a, y for b, … The leading spaces in the key are ignored.
b is seen first (a) and a second (b). Using a letter's raw index in the key would map a to d, because the repeated b's would be counted.

constraints: key and message contain only lowercase letters and spaces
key contains every lowercase letter at least once

args: pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs
the five boxing wizards jump quickly
the five boxing wizards jump quickly
the five boxing wizards jump quickly
pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs
pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs

hints: Build the translation table once, then the message is a single pass.
Walk the key with a counter that starts at 'a'. When you meet a letter that is not in the table yet, map it to the counter and advance the counter.
Skip spaces and letters already in the table. In the message, leave spaces untouched and replace every letter through the table.

explain.intuition:
The key is a recipe for a 26-entry lookup table. The only rule people miss is that a letter gets its slot the first time it appears; later copies and spaces do not consume a slot. So keep a counter of how many distinct letters you have seen and assign the next plain letter only when you meet a new one.

After that, decoding is a plain map over the characters of the message, the same way you would translate keys through a lookup object in the UI.
steps: Create an empty table and set next = 'a'.
For each character of key: if it is a letter not yet in the table, map it to next and advance next.
Build the answer by walking message: spaces stay, letters go through the table.
pitfalls: Using a letter's index in the key as its slot. Repeated letters and spaces before it push that index too far.
Overwriting a mapping when a letter appears again. Only the first sighting counts.
Mapping spaces in the key or in the message. They are not part of the cipher.

complexity.space: O(1) for the table, O(|message|) for the output

solutions.title: Search the key for every letter
solutions.idea: For each letter of the message, scan the key and count how many distinct letters appear before its first sighting. That count is its plain letter.

solutions.title: Build the table once
solutions.idea: One pass over the key fills a letter-to-letter table on first sightings. One pass over the message translates.

followups: Write the encoder: given the same key and a plain message, produce the cipher text.
The key may be missing some letters. Map the unseen ones to the remaining plain letters in alphabetical order. What changes?
